analysis.one_liner: Replaces the consumer bankruptcy system with a single simplified chapter that makes it cheaper and easier to erase debt.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the Senate on September 28, 2022 with one cosponsor, referred to the Finance Committee, and never received a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would throw out the current consumer bankruptcy chapters and replace them with a single 'Chapter 10' for people with less than $7.5 million in debt. Debtors would owe only what their income and assets allow — many would pay nothing and get their debts wiped out immediately — and the bill would let people modify home mortgages and car loans to market value and discharge private student loans like other debts. It would also cut paperwork and filing costs and create a Consumer Bankruptcy Ombuds at the consumer financial regulator.
analysis.who_benefits: People buried in debt — especially those facing medical bills, job loss, foreclosure, or unpayable private student loans — would get a faster, cheaper bankruptcy path, with many paying little or nothing and still wiping out their debts. Rent-to-own customers, car owners, and homeowners facing foreclosure would also get new protections.

how_it_helps.text: Debtors with no ability to pay could get an immediate discharge of their debts without filing a payment plan.
Homeowners could modify mortgages in bankruptcy — including curing defaults without penalty interest or late fees — which current law forbids for primary residences.
Private student loan debt would become dischargeable like most other debt, and car loans could be rewritten to the vehicle's actual market value.
The bill aims to cut paperwork and filing costs, letting people pay attorneys over time and closing loopholes the wealthy use to shield assets.
It creates a Consumer Bankruptcy Ombuds at the CFPB and voids pre-dispute arbitration and class-action waivers tied to property in a bankruptcy plan.

analysis.who_pays: Lenders and other creditors would recover less from bankrupt debtors: credit card issuers and other unsecured creditors, private student loan lenders, mortgage and auto lenders facing loan modifications, and the bankruptcy attorneys whose fees depend on a complex system.

drawbacks.text: Lenders and other unsecured creditors would recover less, since the bill repeals Chapter 7 liquidation for individuals and caps what debtors must repay, and creditors argue this raises the price of credit for everyone else.

The bill replaces the entire existing consumer bankruptcy framework with a largely untested Chapter 10, a major transition whose administrative effects on courts and trustees were never examined in committee.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For debtors, the benefits would be large: cheaper, simpler filings, mortgage and car-loan modifications, and student-loan discharge. The costs fall on lenders and on unsecured creditors, who would recover less, and there is a real design risk in a brand-new single-chapter system replacing decades of settled Chapter 7 and Chapter 13 practice; the bill never advanced far enough to be tested in committee hearings, so its workability is unproven.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee in late September 2022; the committee never acted on it and the Congress ended without any vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on September 28, 2022, in the final months of the 117th Congress.
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which took no further action.
Only one Democratic senator cosponsored, and no Republican.
The bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, without a hearing or a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit card issuers, private student lenders, mortgage servicers, and other creditors keep the existing bankruptcy rules that make erasing debt slow and expensive.

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and drafted its Chapter 10 overhaul of consumer bankruptcy.

for.name: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after it was referred.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had only Democratic support — Warren, Whitehouse, and one other Democratic cosponsor — with no Republican cosponsors and no action by the Senate.

industries.industry: Consumer lenders and credit card issuers
industries.note: Unsecured debts would be dischargeable faster and cheaper, with a six-year limit between discharges and a formula capping what debtors must repay, cutting recoveries.
The bill makes their loans dischargeable in bankruptcy like ordinary debt, removing the special protection they have enjoyed since 2005.
Homeowners could strip penalties, cure defaults, and restructure mortgages in bankruptcy, reducing foreclosures and what lenders collect.
Streamlined no-payment cases and reduced paperwork would shrink the fees and filings that support much of the consumer bankruptcy bar, though the bill lets debtors pay lawyers through plans.
